title: Replicas, Partitions, and Shards

sections.title: Data Access Patterns and Storage Selection
Read Replicas and the Write-Ahead Log

html:
Chapter 5 reduced repeated catalog reads by caching popular data. As Baodium’s traffic increased, however, customers requested more distinct products, search filters, and account records, so a large share of the traffic still reached the primary database. The engineers proposed read replicas to distribute those queries.

The replicas reduced read traffic on the primary, but soon customer support received reports of shipping addresses appearing to revert after an update. A customer could save a new address, reopen the account page, and briefly see the old one. A later refresh displayed the new value. The database had accepted the change. The first read reached a replica before it had replayed that write.1

The behavior will be familiar if you have posted a comment, refreshed the page, and briefly seen it disappear. For Baodium’s address form, the team could not promise that an immediate read would reflect the saved change while routing that read to an asynchronous replica. The requirement for each read determines whether replica routing is appropriate. The same access patterns also influence the partitioning and sharding decisions later in the chapter.

Data Access Patterns and Storage Selection

Before adding copies of a database, the team asked whether every kind of data belonged in it at all. A new application may need one store for customer records, another way to search large catalogs, and a place to retain uploaded documents. The first design decision comes from how the application reads and changes that data. A database choice made before those operations are known can force the team into expensive queries or unsafe update paths.

Baodium’s order checkout needs a transaction that changes several related records while enforcing order and payment invariants. PostgreSQL provides transactions, foreign keys, and indexes for those operations. Catalog browsing has different demands, such as text relevance, faceted filters, and high-volume searches. A dedicated search index can serve those queries, with Catalog Service continuing to own authoritative product updates. Product photographs are large immutable objects, making object storage a better fit than storing their bytes in relational rows.

A key-value database becomes a candidate when most operations retrieve or update records by known keys and the required transactions and secondary queries fit its guarantees. A relational model is often the simpler start when data relationships and transactional changes are central. Neither label settles the decision by itself. We still need representative queries, data volume, update frequency, retention, freshness limits, and evidence from a realistic load test.

An index or projection can lag the owning database. For example, a product may be removed from sale while an older search result still displays it. The search result is a discovery aid. The checkout path must verify current sale eligibility at the authoritative boundary. The replication and ownership sections below explain how that distinction is enforced.

Primary Database Constraints

When a database struggles, the first thing to establish is whether you store too much data or receive too many concurrent queries. The two sound similar, but they call for different changes. Figure Figure shows how many sources of work share one connection pool.

A large historical table may make archiving and index maintenance expensive while receiving few customer queries. A much smaller table may serve thousands of requests per second and compete heavily for database resources. More storage will not fix connection or lock contention, so the first job is to find out whether the constraint comes from data volume, query execution, connection demand, or transactions waiting on other work.

At Baodium, individual catalog queries were still inexpensive, but connection-acquisition time rose steadily as more requests competed for the primary. That pointed to a concurrency problem without explaining its cause. Using the measurements from Chapters 1 and 2, the engineers checked connection occupancy, transaction duration, other callers, and database CPU and I/O, because a pool can fill for several reasons, and replicas would not fix all of them.

The investigation showed that eligible catalog reads were using a large share of the primary’s capacity. Writes and other work that required the primary competed with those reads, so serving those reads elsewhere would leave more capacity for the operations that needed the primary. Table Table summarizes the options the team considered.

The techniques change different parts of the data path.
Technique What changes Application responsibility
Read replicas Additional copies serve eligible reads. Freshness, routing, and fallback.
Table partitioning Rows are organized into separate tables under one logical table. Partition-aware queries, keys, and maintenance.
Sharding Separate databases own subsets of records. Ownership routing, cross-shard work, and migration.

You can combine these techniques. A shard can contain partitioned tables and have its own replicas, and there is no required order for adopting them. For the catalog read workload, replicas addressed the immediate problem without dividing write ownership, so partitioning and sharding each needed their own justification, which the later sections develop.

Read Replicas and the Write-Ahead Log

A read replica maintains a copy of the database and serves queries against it. In the PostgreSQL setup used in this chapter, one primary accepts all application writes, and physical streaming replication updates the replicas continuously (Figure Figure).

To see how a replica tracks the primary, imagine sharing a spreadsheet with a colleague in another office. Instead of sending the whole file every time, you send them a list of every change you make, and they apply each change to their own copy. Their copy is only as current as the last change they have received and applied. A PostgreSQL replica works in much the same way. The primary records every change in its write-ahead log, or WAL, before the changed data pages are written to durable storage, and the same log lets the primary recover after a crash. A replica receives that log over the network and replays it against its own copy of the data. Other database systems implement replication differently, but the question is similar. When can a reader observe a committed change?

That gives you three stages between a write on the primary and a query on a replica that can see it.

Generation.

The primary produces WAL records for the changes.

Receipt and persistence.

The standby receives the WAL and writes it to disk according to its durability and acknowledgment settings.

Replay.

The standby applies the changes, so that later query snapshots can see them.

Your colleague having the list of changes in their inbox is not the same as having applied them, and in the same way, a replica that has received the WAL may still return old data. For read routing, replay progress is the number to check.

With asynchronous replication, the primary can confirm a committed write before any replica has received or replayed it.2 The customer at the start of the chapter read the account page during that interval.

Replicas also do work beyond serving customer queries. They have to receive and replay changes, maintain their own database state, and read data into memory. Heavy queries compete with that work, so an extra replica does not give you the same capacity as an idle copy of the primary would.

Read Consistency Requirements

One question sorts almost every read in an application. What goes wrong if this result is a second out of date? For a product description, almost nothing does. For the address the customer has just saved, the customer loses confidence that the change worked. For a decision about whether stock is available to reserve, the business may sell something it does not have. Before you choose a connection for a read, decide which of these it is. Figure Figure shows the window during which a replica read can return old data.

Baodium classified reads by the operation they supported (Table Table).

Read routing depends on the result the caller requires.
Read requirement Example Routing approach
Accepted replica delay Browsing a product description. Use an eligible replica under the route’s policy.
Read-your-writes Viewing a newly saved address. Return committed state, use the primary, or verify replica replay progress.
Authoritative transaction Reserving available inventory. Execute through the owning service and database transaction.

This classification belongs close to the query or the service operation. A global rule that sends every SELECT to a replica cannot distinguish a browsing page from a check inside a purchase transaction. And a transaction that reads some state and then updates it must use the same database transaction throughout. Sending its reads to a replica can invalidate the assumptions its write depends on.

Authoritative Reads and Transactions

Many engineers assume that sending the inventory check to the primary, rather than a replica, protects the last unit of a product from being sold twice. The primary gives you the latest committed value, which removes replica delay, but two requests can still read that same value at the same moment. Suppose two customers try to reserve the last unit at the same moment. Both can read an available quantity of one before either of them submits a reservation, and both then go ahead. What the application needs is an atomic reservation, not a current read and then an unprotected write.

If the statement returns a row, it reserved a unit. If it returns no row, it made no reservation, which can mean that the product does not exist or that none is available, depending on the surrounding operation. A production reservation also records its operation identity and reservation details in the same transaction, so that a repeated request cannot reduce the stock a second time, as Chapter 3 described.

Primary routing and transaction correctness solve two related problems. The first decides which database is authoritative, and the second decides how concurrent operations may change its records. Payment and inventory access still go through the services that own those operations, and adding a replica is no reason for another service to bypass that ownership.

Read-Your-Writes

Return to the customer from the start of the chapter. The guarantee that customer needed has a name, read-your-writes: after you change something, your own later reads show the change, even if other people’s reads may not yet. It was first described as one of several session guarantees for replicated systems in the 1990s, and it is still the one users notice most.

The simplest way to provide it is to return the committed address from the write operation itself. The page can show that result without another database query, which avoids replica lag entirely for that first response.

A later request is harder, because it may reach another application instance or come from another device. Sending that read to the primary satisfies the requirement, as long as the query takes its snapshot after the write committed. Another common approach is to send a user’s reads to the primary for a fixed time after they write. Rails, for example, can switch reads automatically in this way, with a default delay of two seconds. A timer reduces stale reads, but it offers no assurance, because replica lag can last longer than the delay you chose.

A more precise approach returns a replication position with the committed write, a bit like a receipt number. In PostgreSQL, the primary can report its current WAL position with pg_current_wal_lsn(), and a replica reports how far it has replayed with pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(). The router uses a replica only after it has replayed past the position of the write. Otherwise, it waits within a deadline, uses permitted primary access, or returns an unavailable result.

The position must cover the commit, and the query must take its snapshot after the replay condition is met, because an earlier snapshot could still return the old state. Positions also belong to one database history. After a failover, PostgreSQL starts a new timeline, and the application cannot compare positions from different histories without checking how they relate.

This extra machinery pays off when sending these reads to the primary becomes expensive. For a modest number of account updates, returning the committed state and using the primary for the few sensitive reads after it is usually easier to operate.

Decision review

Which reads may use a replica?

Browsing traffic is saturating the primary. Two replicas are available, and replication lag is usually under a second. Four read paths are candidates, the product detail page, the “items in your cart” panel, the availability message shown next to the Add to Cart button, and the order confirmation page shown immediately after a purchase.

Send all four to replicas. The lag is under a second, and no customer notices a second.

Send the product page, the availability message, and the cart panel to replicas, give the cart panel read-your-writes after a change, and serve the confirmation page from the primary.

Send only the product page, because it receives the most requests.

Sort them by what a stale result costs rather than by traffic volume, using the question from earlier in this section.

The confirmation page is the clearest case against A. It is read right after the customer’s own write, which is the window in which a replica is most likely not to have applied it. The customer completes a purchase and is shown an order that does not seem to exist. Read-your-writes is a requirement here, and returning the committed order from the checkout response is the simplest way to meet it.

The cart panel can use a replica for ordinary reads, but a read immediately after the customer changes a quantity needs the same read-your-writes treatment, using one of the approaches described above.

The availability message may look as if it needs the primary, but it is only a hint for browsing. As Chapter 5 established, the reservation at checkout is the authoritative check, and Section Section explains why even a primary read would not stop two customers from taking the last unit. A message that is a second out of date is acceptable, as long as checkout handles the rare case where the item is gone.

That makes B the right choice. C leaves capacity unused for no benefit.

Replica Eligibility and Fallback

The database team added two replicas for browsing queries whose freshness policy allowed them. The router chose among replicas that were reachable, had current monitoring information, and met the route’s eligibility criteria. The freshness of the monitoring information matters as much as its content. A replica that reported very little lag several minutes ago may have disconnected since then, and that old sample must not make it eligible.

Each routing observation records when the sample was taken, the measured replay progress, and the connection’s health. A background observer collects these values, so that customer requests do not each run a monitoring query.

Interpreting Lag Measurements

Imagine your dashboard shows a replica as 30 seconds behind at three o’clock in the morning, and the alert is about to page someone. Before anyone gets out of bed, you need to know what that number measures.

Replication positions describe progress through the WAL. A difference in bytes tells you how much log is waiting to be applied, but not how many seconds or transactions that represents. A heartbeat gives you a time-based estimate. The primary updates a row at a regular interval, and an observer reads that row from each replica. The estimate then depends on how often the heartbeat runs, how often samples are collected, and how clocks are handled.

Another common time-based measure uses pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(), which reports when the last replayed transaction was committed. On a busy system, the time since then is a reasonable estimate of lag. At three in the morning, though, when almost no writes are arriving, the replica may have applied everything there is, and the number rises only because no new transactions have arrived. The replica in the example may be fully caught up, and paging someone would be a mistake. “Forty megabytes behind” and “thirty seconds behind” are not interchangeable, and you need to know which one your dashboard shows.

No lag measure, however accurate, tells you that one particular write is visible. A previous lag sample or a low average cannot satisfy a strict read-your-writes requirement, which needs evidence tied to that write or a route to the authoritative database.

Bounded Primary Fallback

When every replica is unavailable, the obvious response is to send their reads to the primary, and it is also the dangerous one.

Suppose the replicas normally serve 80 percent of a browsing workload and the primary serves the other 20 percent. If every replica read falls back to the primary, that part of the primary’s traffic becomes five times its usual rate. Requests succeed at first, but their reads now compete with the writes, reconciliation, and other required reads the primary has to handle. You saw the same situation with a failed cache in Chapter 5. Unrestricted fallback can turn a replica outage into a primary outage.

The database team treated fallback as a workload with its own admission limit. When that allocation was used up, the route returned its approved reduced or unavailable result. The routing logic can be written without putting every database detail in the handler.

The admission methods return either an admitted target or a rejection, so they do not hide another unbounded queue, and their permits cover the query until it finishes and its resources are released. A route that requires the primary uses its own admission path, and a route that requires a write position also checks that position before it runs a query on a replica. This simplified example covers browsing reads that only need operational replica eligibility.

Whatever happens, the router must not relax a route’s freshness requirement because all of the preferred targets are unavailable. If a route accepts older results, that has to be part of its policy from the start.

Replica Failover and Recovery

Replicas have a second job that has nothing to do with read capacity. If the primary fails, one of them can be promoted to take its place. Read scaling and failover use related infrastructure, but they have different requirements. With asynchronous replication, a promoted standby may be missing writes that the old primary had already confirmed to clients. The question during failover is which confirmed commits are present and durable on the candidate. Replay delay alone does not decide how much data could be lost, because WAL that has been received and stored durably, but not yet replayed, can still be applied before the new primary starts serving requests.

Synchronous replication makes a write wait for acknowledgment from a standby before it returns, and the selected mode decides what that acknowledgment covers. In PostgreSQL, synchronous_commit set to remote_apply waits until the standby has applied the commit, so later snapshots on that standby can see it. The default on setting waits only until the WAL is durably stored on the standby, which does not give the same immediate read guarantee, and an asynchronous replica elsewhere may still be behind. The cost is extra commit latency and a policy decision about what to do when the required standbys are unavailable. Lowering the acknowledgment requirement during an outage changes your durability contract, so it should be a deliberate decision, not an automatic one.

Failover also has to stop the old primary from accepting writes once a replacement has been promoted. Picture two people who each believe they are the only one allowed to update a shared ledger. Every entry either of them makes from then on may conflict with the other’s. This situation has a vivid name, split brain, and preventing it is called fencing, because it puts a barrier around the old writer so that it cannot accept writes, even if it restarts still configured as the primary. Changing the routing is not enough if old connections can still reach it. The deployment needs a way to fence the former primary and to confirm the new one’s authority, using the same token idea you saw for leases in Chapter 3.

Replication does not replace backups, because a mistaken delete is replayed on every replica as faithfully as any other change. Recovering to an earlier point in time requires backups and the retained change history, and only regular restore tests show that recovery works.

Field note

GitHub, October 2018

A 43-second network interruption separated GitHub’s East Coast network hub from its primary data center. The Orchestrator tool promoted databases on the West Coast. The former primaries contained writes that had not yet replicated west, while the new primaries went on to accept writes of their own. Returning to the former primaries required reconciling two divergent histories.

GitHub put data integrity first during recovery and paused work such as webhook delivery and Pages builds. Its report describes 24 hours and 11 minutes of degraded service and states that no user data was lost, with some reconciliation still in progress when the report was published. Promotion chose a new writer before anyone had worked out the complete write history. A failover test has to examine confirmed writes and the fencing of the former writer, not just the promotion procedure.

Source: published incident report.

Point-in-Time Recovery and Restore Testing

A database migration can delete the wrong month’s orders and commit successfully. The replicas then apply the same deletion. If the team promotes one of those replicas, the orders are still missing. The recovery plan needs an earlier copy of the data.

For PostgreSQL, point-in-time recovery combines a base backup with archived write-ahead log records. An operator can restore into a new database environment and replay the retained log up to a chosen point before the deletion.3

Restoring the earlier copy introduces another decision. Orders created after the mistaken deletion would disappear too if the team replaced production with the backup. We may need to recover selected records from the restored copy and reconcile operations that completed in the meantime. That is why a restore plan needs both a recovery-point objective (RPO), the acceptable loss of committed changes, and a recovery-time objective (RTO), the acceptable time before the service is usable again.

A practical rehearsal restores an isolated copy, verifies that the application can read it, checks that the expected orders exist, and measures how long reconciliation and reopening the service take. That rehearsal can uncover missing WAL segments, an unreadable backup, or an application that cannot start with the restored schema. Recovery raises identical concerns after the accidental deletion of a SaaS tenant, a message archive, or a metadata catalog.

Table Partitioning

So far, every problem in this chapter has been about reads. The orders table had a different problem, and replicas could not help with it. The table contained six years of customer orders, and a new retention policy required orders to be deleted after 24 months. The monthly archival job that enforced the policy deleted expired rows one batch at a time. Each run took most of a night, produced a large volume of WAL that the replicas then had to replay, and left bloated indexes behind it. Any system with time-ordered data, such as logs, metrics, events, or transactions, eventually meets the same problem.

Think of a filing cabinet in which every order is filed in one long drawer. Throwing away last year’s orders means going through the drawer and pulling out each old folder one at a time. If the cabinet instead had one drawer per month, you could empty a whole drawer in one step. That is the idea behind partitioning. It divides one logical table into separate physical tables according to a partition key, such as the month an order was created. When a query includes conditions on that key, PostgreSQL can skip the partitions that cannot contain matching rows, which is called partition pruning.

The partition key should match the queries or maintenance operation that is expensive, so the team started with the operations rather than with the table.

Table Table compares three candidate keys against those operations. Before you read it, try to guess which key serves all three operations best.

If you guessed one, the table has a surprise for you. No key serves all three. created_at removes the archival work and narrows the report to one partition, but it does nothing for the point lookup, and the rest of the design has to deal with that gap. This is the usual situation with partitioning, and with indexing in general. You choose the key for the most expensive work and design around the rest.

The upper boundary is exclusive, so the next partition begins at that timestamp. Writing the time zone in the boundaries avoids depending on how a session would interpret a timestamp without one.

For the lookup, the application can include the creation month in the order reference it gives customers, maintain a directory that maps each order to its partition, or accept that occasional lookups probe every partition. With about 25 monthly partitions under the retention policy and support lookups at a few requests per second, the database team measured the cost of probing them all before deciding whether a directory was justified.

Identity and Constraints

The primary key in the example includes the partition key, because PostgreSQL requires every unique constraint on a partitioned table to include the partition key. The constraint now protects less than its name suggests. The database now enforces uniqueness of the pair (order_id, created_at), but not uniqueness of order_id on its own across all dates.

If the application needs the database to guarantee that order IDs are globally unique, it needs another mechanism. One option is a nonpartitioned order directory with a unique order ID, written in the same transaction as the order itself. That directory can also store the creation month, which closes the point-lookup gap from Table Table. The directory adds one indexed insert per order, plus its own storage. At Baodium’s order rate, that cost was small, but it still had to be included in the capacity estimate, and the rule tying the two records together had to be tested.

Partition Operations

A partition must exist before rows arrive for its range. Without a matching partition or a deliberate default partition, the insert fails, so you do not want to discover on the first day of a month that the maintenance job never created that month’s partition. The database team created partitions three months ahead and alerted when fewer than two future partitions were left. Extensions such as pg_partman can automate this kind of scheduled creation.

Archival became a metadata operation, the equivalent of emptying a whole drawer. Detaching an expired partition replaced the nightly batch deletes, removed most of their WAL, and left no bloat in the indexes of the current partitions. PostgreSQL’s DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY reduces the locking this requires, though the operation still has to be coordinated with backups, references, and the retention policy.

Partitioning reduced maintenance work and, where pruning applied, query work. It did not add a database server or spread writes across machines. The release test checked query plans for the three operations above, the first insert into a new range, and a partition detach under production-like load.

Sharding and Data Ownership

Replicas spread reads, and partitioning organized data within one database. Neither helps when a single database can no longer sustain the write rate. The sharding discussion began in a design review, with an engineer asking which database would own the next write to merchant order MO-48192.

Each confirmed checkout produced one merchant order for every merchant in the cart, published through the outbox from Chapter 3. Merchants accepted, shipped, refunded, and settled those orders through the merchant portal, and every step wrote to the merchant order, its line items, its fulfillment state, and the merchant’s payout ledger, all on one primary. In a multi-tenant SaaS application, a few large tenants can produce most of the writes and expensive queries, creating the same imbalance.

Two measurements forced the question. Merchant-order writes peaked at about 3,000 per second, against roughly 4,000 that the primary had sustained in workload tests after index and batching improvements. And when the largest merchants ran end-of-day settlement or bulk refunds, their transactions took locks and consumed I/O that every other merchant depended on. Replicas could not help with either problem, because both were about writes.

Sharding assigns subsets of records to separate databases, each with its own write path. A familiar comparison is a bank with several branches, where each customer’s account belongs to a single branch. Deposits and withdrawals happen at the account’s own branch, and only a transfer between accounts at two different branches needs the branches to coordinate. With sharding, the application has to determine, for every write, which branch owns the record, in every process and consistently across deployments, and it has to be able to change that assignment later without rewriting every stored reference.

You may be wondering whether a distributed database, such as Citus, Vitess, or CockroachDB, would make all of this unnecessary. These systems do take over much of the routing and rebalancing. They still ask you to choose a distribution key, or they partition data by key ranges, and the issues in the rest of this section, about which transactions can run on one node and where the hot spots appear, come back in that form. Because sharding is so hard to reverse, the database team considered it only after caching, replicas, and partitioning had been applied where they fit.

Choosing the Shard Key

The shard key decides which transactions can run inside one database, in the same way that the bank’s choice of branch decides which transfers are local. Social networks usually shard by user, SaaS products by tenant, and messaging systems by conversation, each because their most important transactions are scoped that way. The Baodium team listed the merchant-order operations by frequency and correctness requirement, then tested three candidate keys against them (Table Table). Try picking one yourself before reading the analysis below.

merchant_order_id spreads writes evenly, but it turns settlement into a distributed transaction across every shard. Settlement transfers money, so that was the operation the team was least willing to make cross-shard.

merchant_id scopes every operation to one merchant on one shard, including settlement. The cost is that each merchant’s whole workload concentrates on a single shard, so one very large merchant can dominate it. Social networks know this as the celebrity problem, where one account with millions of followers produces more traffic than thousands of ordinary ones.

(merchant_id, sub-bucket) hashes each merchant across 16 sub-buckets. It spreads a large merchant’s writes, but settlement and the portal list then have to cross up to 16 buckets.

The database team chose merchant_id. The most important write transaction was scoped to a single merchant, and the team accepted the large-merchant hot spot as a known risk to measure rather than a reason to give up local settlement. Section Section examines that risk.

The choice had two further consequences. Operations that spanned merchants, such as an operator’s view of all recent orders, now needed several shards. And uniqueness changed. A merchant-scoped order number could still be enforced by one shard, but a carrier tracking number that had to be unique across all merchants could not be enforced by any single shard, so that rule needed a separate directory with its own unique index.

A transaction that genuinely spans shards needs a defined coordination procedure, either a distributed transaction or a saga of durable steps with recovery and compensation, as Chapter 3 described.

Routing and Shard Assignment

The router must produce the same assignment in every process and every deployment. A hash function whose seed changes between process starts is unsuitable for persistent placement. Python’s built-in hash() for strings is one example, because it is randomized for each process. If you used it, the same merchant could be sent to a different shard after every restart. Figure Figure shows the route from a key to a database.

A fixed modulo over the number of physical shards is easy to implement, but consider what happens when you add a ninth shard to eight. Changing the divisor reassigns most keys, and every reassigned key has to be copied before the new rule can be used. A fixed set of virtual buckets avoids this by separating the assignment of records from their physical placement. Consistent hashing, used by systems such as Amazon’s Dynamo and Apache Cassandra, solves the same problem in a different way, by placing keys and servers on a ring so that adding a server reassigns only the keys next to it.

The number of buckets and the way IDs are canonicalized are part of the persisted routing contract, and changing either one requires a migration. Section Section explains the merchant override.

The directory maps each bucket to a database and an ownership version, called an epoch. Reassigning a bucket changes one directory entry instead of every record’s assignment. The directory is also a dependency. Routers cache it along with its version, and each database stores the epoch it currently owns for each bucket, so that it can reject writes routed with an outdated entry. This is the fencing idea from the failover section, and it works like the lease tokens from Chapter 3.

Uneven Load Across Shards

Try a quick estimate before you read on. The database team started with eight shards, each tested at about 900 writes per second, and merchant orders peaked at 3,000 writes per second. How much more traffic could the fleet take?

If you multiplied eight by 900, you probably said 7,200 writes per second, well over twice the current peak. The actual figure was far smaller, because equal numbers of rows do not mean equal demand on each database, and the choice of merchant_id made that concrete in the first few weeks.

The largest merchant produced about 18 percent of all merchant-order writes. At the peak of 3,000 writes per second, that merchant alone generated 540. The other 2,460 spread across the eight shards at roughly 308 each, so the shard that contained the large merchant handled about 848 writes per second, against a fleet average of 375. That shard would reach its tested limit of 900 if total traffic rose by only about six percent. The busiest shard sets the limit for the whole fleet, whatever the average says.

The team measured query rate, transaction cost, connection occupancy, and storage for each shard, and then considered three responses.

  • Reassign the other buckets away from the hot shard. That removes at most 308 writes per second and leaves the large merchant as the shard’s main load.

  • Give the merchant a dedicated shard through a merchant-level override in the directory, checked before the bucket entry. Its 540 writes per second fit within one database’s tested 900, and settlement is still local.

  • Split the merchant across sub-buckets, as in the third candidate key. That would turn its settlement into a cross-bucket operation.

The database team chose the dedicated shard. If a single merchant ever came close to one database’s tested write limit, the split key and a redesigned settlement procedure would become necessary, and the team recorded that threshold as a review trigger.

Cross-Shard Queries

Now picture a page that shows the latest 100 merchant orders across all merchants, when those orders are spread over eight databases.

A query that includes the shard key goes to one database, but a query without it may need every shard. Sending that query to every shard concurrently and combining the results is called scatter-gather. For the operator page, there is no need to fetch every recent row from every shard and sort them in application memory. Each shard returns its own latest 100 under a common ordering, and the application merges the candidates, much as a referee might combine the top finishers from several heats to find the overall winners. The ordering needs a tie-breaker, such as creation time and then order ID, and pagination needs a cursor so that the next page does not scan the same rows again. Separate shard queries also do not share one snapshot, so the page’s contract has to say how concurrent writes may appear.

Fan-out needs limits across requests, not just within one. If each page request starts eight worker threads, a busy page can produce hundreds of active queries. A shared, bounded executor, per-shard admission, and one deadline for the whole request bound the combined work, using the techniques from Chapter 4. As that chapter also explained, giving up on a waiting future does not necessarily stop a running query, so a database-side limit, such as PostgreSQL’s statement_timeout, or a cancel request has to stop the work on the shard.

The result also needs a rule for completeness. An exploratory dashboard may show partial results with the missing shards identified, but a reconciliation total cannot be reported as complete when one shard failed to respond.

Bounded Cross-Shard Queries

The operator page ran a few times a minute, so eight shard queries per request were acceptable. Carrier tracking updates were a different matter. Each update arrived keyed only by tracking number, which does not identify the merchant.

At the peak of 300 tracking updates per second, scatter-gather would send 2,400 shard queries per second before retries, and seven out of every eight would find nothing. Adding shards would only increase that number. A tracking-number directory, written when an order ships, costs one indexed insert per shipment and turns each update into one directory lookup and one shard write. Baodium shipped about 40 orders per second at peak, so the directory replaced 2,400 fan-out reads per second with about 340 directory operations, and it also enforced the global uniqueness of tracking numbers.

In general, the cost of fan-out scales with the request rate multiplied by the number of shards. A maintained directory or read model costs its update rate, plus its storage and the delay before updates appear. When the first number is larger than the second, and the read model’s delay fits the path’s freshness requirement, the read model is the cheaper design. Large systems lean heavily on this idea, maintaining secondary indexes and lookup tables so that common requests avoid fan-out.

Resharding and Ownership Transfer

Transferring the large merchant to its dedicated shard raised a practical problem. The merchant’s data had to be copied while the merchant went on writing to it. It is a little like moving house while the family is still living there. You cannot stop everyone for the length of the relocation, but there has to be one moment when the new house becomes the official address.

This was Baodium’s first ownership transfer under live writes. The new directory entry could not be published until the destination had a complete, verified copy of the merchant’s data and had been given write authority. The procedure had five stages.

  1. Copy. Copy the merchant’s rows while the source shard goes on serving, and record the source change position at which the copy began.

  2. Catch up. Capture changes made after that position and apply them to the destination until the gap is small.

  3. Fence. Mark the merchant as transferring on the source, which rejects new writes for it, and let in-flight transactions finish.

  4. Final apply and verify. Record the final source change position, apply changes through it, and compare row totals and per-order checksums.

  5. Transfer authority. Increment the ownership epoch, publish the directory entry, and allow the destination to accept writes.

The merchant had about 140 million rows to copy. At the tested transfer rate, the initial copy took about 93 minutes. Changes committed during that copy still needed replay. Because the change applier processed more updates than the merchant generated, the lag closed in roughly eleven minutes. Only then did the team pause new writes briefly, verify the destination, and transfer ownership. The longer transfer happened while customers continued using the source shard.

The former owner has to enforce its loss of authority itself. Publishing a new directory entry is not enough while some routers still have cached routes or open connections.

A router that receives StaleRoute refreshes its directory entry and retries under the operation’s original identity, so the retry cannot apply the change twice.

Rollback becomes harder once the destination has accepted writes. Pointing routes back to the source would lose those writes unless they were copied back through another controlled transfer. The migration tests covered a process failure during the copy, a delayed router cache refresh, duplicate requests across the fence, and an interruption between stages 4 and 5. At every stage, the test checked that there was a single known owner, not only that the row totals matched.

Read Routing and Failover Tests

Each change to the database layout needs a test aimed at the new failure path it introduces.

For replicas, the database team paused replay after committing a customer update and checked read-your-writes behavior, which recreated the stale address from the start of the chapter on purpose. The team also tested expired monitoring samples and the loss of every eligible replica, and primary fallback had to fit within its allocation while required writes continued. Replica query tests included replay contention and queries canceled by recovery conflicts. PostgreSQL settings such as max_standby_streaming_delay and hot_standby_feedback decide whether a long query on a replica delays replay or affects cleanup on the primary, so reporting queries need particular attention.

For partitioning, the team inspected the query plans for archival, the monthly report, and the point lookup, and tested the first insert into a new time range. Uniqueness requirements were checked separately from date-range performance.

For sharding, the test data reproduced the production distribution of merchant sizes, including the merchant with 18 percent of writes, because a balanced synthetic dataset would have hidden the hot shard. The tests covered an unavailable shard, incomplete fan-out results, stale routes after a transfer, and tracking-directory lookups for orders that had not shipped yet.

Production measurements used the same boundaries. Replica health included replay progress and the age of each sample, and routing metrics showed which read classes reached each target and how much primary fallback was in use. Partition measurements included query plans, storage, and detach duration. Shard measurements included each shard’s write rate against its tested limit, connection occupancy, errors, and the share of traffic coming from the largest merchant on each shard. A fleet-wide average would have reported 375 writes per second while one shard was handling 848.

Finally, the team recorded the writes exposed during each failover, the results of restore tests, and the ownership epochs during migrations, so that an engineer investigating any incident could see where the data was and which writes had been accepted.

Regional Metadata Write Authority

These decisions come up in systems that have nothing to do with shopping. Imagine a document service with customers in North America and Europe. Users fetch a document by ID, list their tenant’s documents, rename a file, and share it with a colleague. The file bytes can live in object storage, but the metadata, the titles, owners, and permissions, needs authenticated updates, indexes, and a clear rule for who may write each record.

As with Baodium’s orders, the design starts from the operations. Fetching by ID uses the primary key. Listing a tenant’s documents needs an index that begins with the tenant and matches the sort order and pagination the API promises. Sharing a file updates an access record and an audit record together, so it needs a transaction. And the file and its metadata must be consistent. A file sitting in object storage proves nothing about whether its metadata transaction committed, so committed metadata points to an object the application can verify, and orphaned uploads are cleaned up.

A sensible first version uses one transactional database as the metadata authority, read replicas in each region for reads that can tolerate a delay, and object storage for the files. The routing rules come straight from earlier in this chapter. The owner who has just renamed a file expects to see the new name, so that read needs read-your-writes, while a public browse page can accept a little staleness.

A second writable region changes the problem completely. With asynchronous replication, an update acknowledged in one region can be missing in the other after a failure, and if both regions change the same permission record, the application needs conflict rules and a convincing argument that a revoked permission cannot come back. The simpler design gives each tenant one write-owning region and refuses writes briefly when that ownership cannot be confirmed. Transferring a tenant uses an epoch, as in the shard transfer earlier, so an old writer cannot resume after its replacement starts. Chapter 14 applies the same discipline to checkout during a regional failover.

Partitioning by time or tenant helps with maintenance and query locality, and sharding spreads ownership across databases, but neither replaces the access-pattern analysis. A poor shard key can turn every tenant listing into a query across many shards. Start with the simplest design that meets the measured workload and its correctness promises, and make sure you have a tested way to transfer ownership when those conditions change.

Summary

The customer who saw an old address after saving a new one illustrates the central decision in this chapter. A copy of the data is useful only for reads that can tolerate its delay. Before you route a query to a replica, a partition, or a shard, ask what the caller does with the result and how fresh it must be. The routing rule comes from that decision, not from the database topology.

The three techniques solve different problems, and confusing them is expensive. Replicas spread reads but add lag and need a fallback when they fall behind. Partitioning organizes one large table so that old data can be removed and queries can skip what they do not need. Sharding divides ownership of writes across databases, and it brings a routing directory, ownership epochs, hot-shard plans, and a careful transfer procedure with it. Backups are a separate concern again, since a replica faithfully copies a mistaken delete. A good test for any data layout is to trace one important read and one important write through it, then trace them again with a delayed replica and an unavailable shard.

Each of those paths needs evidence that engineers can see during an incident. Chapter 8 is about producing that evidence.
